sections.label: Origins and preparation
sections.note: Matthew 1–4 moves from genealogy and birth narratives through Jesus’ baptism, temptation, and opening proclamation. The text names several settings but gives no continuous route.

sections.label: Teaching and healing
sections.note: Matthew 5–9 gathers the Sermon on the Mount, healings, and calls to follow. These chapters locate activity around Galilee without fixing every episode to a precise site.

sections.label: Mission and parables
sections.note: Matthew 10–13 combines instructions to the twelve, responses to Jesus, and parables of the kingdom. The text does not present a single continuous itinerary.

sections.label: Signs and discipleship
sections.note: Matthew 14–18 recounts signs, Peter’s confession, teaching about discipleship, and community life. Several settings are named, but the section is not a surveyed itinerary.

sections.label: Teaching on the way to Jerusalem
sections.note: Matthew 19–23 describes teaching beyond the Jordan, entry into Jerusalem, and disputes in the temple. The text supports these named settings but not a detailed route between them.

sections.label: Jerusalem, death, and resurrection
sections.note: Matthew 24–28 moves from teaching on the Mount of Olives to the passion, burial, resurrection, and closing commission. Jerusalem is explicit, while the ending’s destination is Galilee; the text does not describe a continuous route.

sections.label: The Galilean ministry begins
sections.note: Mark 1–4 introduces John the Baptist, Jesus’ early Galilean ministry, calls, healings, and parables. The text names places but gives no continuous route.

sections.label: Signs and the disciples’ confession
sections.note: Mark 5–8 recounts healings, feedings, teaching, and the disciples’ growing recognition of Jesus. Events span named regions, but the text does not specify a complete route.

sections.label: Discipleship and the road to Jerusalem
sections.note: Mark 9–12 combines teaching about discipleship with the journey toward Jerusalem and disputes after Jesus’ entry. The broad movement is stated, but intermediate route details are limited.

sections.label: Jerusalem, passion, and resurrection
sections.note: Mark 13–16 moves from the Mount of Olives discourse to events in Jerusalem, the crucifixion, burial, and the empty tomb. The narrative does not resolve every location detail.

sections.label: Birth narratives and the ministry’s opening
sections.note: Luke 1–4 presents birth narratives, Jesus’ childhood visit to Jerusalem, baptism, temptation, and the opening of his ministry in Galilee. Multiple named settings appear, but no continuous route is given.

sections.label: Teaching and signs in Galilee
sections.note: Luke 5–9 follows calls, teaching, healings, the sending of the twelve, and Peter’s confession. The text places much of this ministry in Galilee; exact sites for every episode remain uncertain.

sections.label: Teaching, parables, and meals
sections.note: Luke 10–14 gathers the sending of the seventy, parables, instruction, and meals with named hosts. The chapters do not provide a route for each teaching scene.

sections.label: Parables and the approach to Jerusalem
sections.note: Luke 15–19 includes parables, teaching, and the narrative’s movement toward Jerusalem, with Jesus’ arrival in chapter 19.

sections.label: Jerusalem, resurrection, and departure
sections.note: Luke 20–24 recounts temple teaching, the passion, resurrection appearances, and the closing departure near Bethany. The text names these settings but leaves some spatial details open.

sections.label: The Word and the first signs
sections.note: John 1–4 introduces Jesus, the Cana sign, a Jerusalem visit, and a conversation in Samaria. These distinct settings do not establish one continuous route.

sections.label: Signs and public teaching
sections.note: John 5–10 recounts signs and extended teaching in Jerusalem and Galilee. The narrative shifts between settings without establishing one precise location for every scene.

sections.label: Lazarus and the final public signs
sections.note: John 11–12 centers on Lazarus at Bethany and Jesus’ approach and entry into Jerusalem. The text supplies these place references but not a complete travel trace.

sections.label: The farewell discourse
sections.note: John 13–17 presents the final meal, Jesus’ teaching to the disciples, and prayer before the arrest. The discourse is tied to the narrative’s final-night setting, but the text does not describe the room in detail.

sections.label: Passion and resurrection appearances
sections.note: John 18–21 recounts arrest, trial, crucifixion, burial, and appearances in Jerusalem-area settings and by the Sea of Tiberias. The closing scenes do not provide a full route.

sections.label: Witness begins in Jerusalem
sections.note: Acts 1–7 recounts the ascension, Pentecost, the Jerusalem community, and its early conflicts. Jerusalem is the stated center of these chapters.

sections.label: Judea, Samaria, and Antioch
sections.note: Acts 8–12 describes the message spreading through Judea and Samaria, Cornelius at Caesarea, and the community at Antioch. These are narrative movements among named places, not a surveyed route.

sections.label: Mission from Antioch and the Jerusalem council
sections.note: Acts 13–15 follows a mission from Antioch through several named cities and the council in Jerusalem. The account identifies major stops but does not provide modern route precision.

sections.label: Macedonia, Greece, and Ephesus
sections.note: Acts 16–20 names travel through Macedonia and Greece, including Corinth, and an extended stay at Ephesus. The narrative supports a broad Mediterranean sequence, not precise road or sea tracks.

sections.label: Arrest and hearings in Jerusalem and Caesarea
sections.note: Acts 21–24 recounts Paul’s arrival in Jerusalem, arrest, and hearings after transfer to Caesarea. Both cities are named; the text does not specify every movement within them.

sections.label: The voyage and arrival in Rome
sections.note: Acts 25–28 follows appeals, a sea voyage with named stops and shipwreck, and arrival in Rome. The account supports this broad sequence, while ancient route geometry and some island identifications remain uncertain.

sections.label: The gospel, sin, and faith
sections.note: Romans 1–4 develops the gospel, the shared problem of sin, and justification by faith. The letter addresses believers in Rome, but this does not establish where it was composed.

sections.label: Peace, new life, and the Spirit
sections.note: Romans 5–8 develops peace with God, life in Christ, and life in the Spirit; it presents theological argument rather than travel narrative.

sections.label: Israel, promise, and mercy
sections.note: Romans 9–11 reflects on Israel, promise, and mercy, arguing from Israel’s scriptures rather than narrating a journey.

sections.label: Community life and greetings
sections.note: Romans 12–16 gives practical instruction, travel intentions, and greetings to named people and communities. The letter’s audience is Roman, but these closing references do not document a completed itinerary.

sections.label: Divisions and the wisdom of the cross
sections.note: 1 Corinthians 1–4 addresses divisions in the Corinthian community and contrasts human status with the message of the cross. The letter does not specify where the community met.

sections.label: Community conduct and food questions
sections.note: 1 Corinthians 5–10 responds to questions of conduct, disputes, marriage, food, and communal responsibility. These are instructions to a church, not stages on a journey.

sections.label: Gathering, gifts, and worship
sections.note: 1 Corinthians 11–14 discusses shared worship, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts, and order in the assembly. The letter does not identify a specific meeting place.

sections.label: Resurrection and closing plans
sections.note: 1 Corinthians 15–16 centers on resurrection and closes with collection and travel plans. These plans are not a record of completed travel.

sections.label: Comfort, ministry, and reconciliation
sections.note: 2 Corinthians 1–4 speaks of comfort amid affliction, apostolic ministry, and the message of reconciliation. The letter does not establish where the hardships it recalls occurred.

sections.label: Hope, reconciliation, and generosity
sections.note: 2 Corinthians 5–9 develops hope, reconciliation, and the collection for other believers. The collection connects communities, but the letter gives no route or meeting place for it.

sections.label: Ministry under challenge
sections.note: 2 Corinthians 10–13 defends the writer’s ministry and recounts hardship and weakness. The text gives no specific geographic setting for this argument.

sections.label: The gospel and its source
sections.note: Galatians 1–2 defends the gospel and recounts encounters and recognition among early leaders. The autobiographical references serve the argument and do not supply a complete itinerary.

sections.label: Promise, faith, and freedom
sections.note: Galatians 3–4 argues from faith, promise, and the status of God’s children. The chapters are scriptural reasoning rather than geographical narrative.

sections.label: Living in freedom
sections.note: Galatians 5–6 applies freedom through life in the Spirit, mutual care, and perseverance. No travel scene is described here; the house label indicates a reading-community context, not an inferred address.

sections.label: Blessing and reconciliation
sections.note: Ephesians 1–2 presents blessing in Christ and reconciliation across former divisions. The passage is a theological address to a community, not a report of movement; the passage does not identify a specific Ephesian site.

sections.label: One body and a shared calling
sections.note: Ephesians 3–4 describes a shared calling and unity in one body. This language describes community unity and does not identify a physical gathering place or travel route.

sections.label: New life and steadfastness
sections.note: Ephesians 5–6 gives household instruction and imagery of spiritual struggle. The household language belongs to the letter’s teaching; the letter does not describe a particular room.

sections.label: Thanks and partnership
sections.note: Philippians 1 expresses thanks, partnership in the gospel, and reflection on hardship and service. The letter’s community focus does not establish the writer’s exact location.

sections.label: Humility and faithful living
sections.note: Philippians 2–3 urges humility and perseverance, holding up Christ’s example and the goal of knowing him. These are exhortations to the community rather than travel scenes.

sections.label: Joy, peace, and generosity
sections.note: Philippians 4 closes with instruction on joy, peace, and the community’s material support. The closing thanks are correspondence, not evidence of a particular delivery route or meeting location.

sections.label: Christ and the community
sections.note: Colossians 1 gives thanks for the community and presents the supremacy of Christ. This is an epistolary teaching passage; the passage does not identify a particular gathering site.

sections.label: Fullness and a renewed life
sections.note: Colossians 2–3 warns against being misled and describes a renewed life in Christ through theological and ethical instruction.

sections.label: Prayer and greetings
sections.note: Colossians 4 gives instruction on prayer and speech and closes with greetings and named coworkers. The greetings indicate correspondence across communities, not a complete itinerary or verified scene location.

sections.label: Faith and remembered service
sections.note: 1 Thessalonians 1–2 recalls the community’s reception of the message and the writer’s earlier service among them. It recalls past relations but gives no complete route.

sections.label: Encouragement and hope
sections.note: 1 Thessalonians 3–4 reports encouragement and gives instruction about holy living and hope for the dead. The letter frames these concerns for a community; no physical journey is the subject of this unit.

sections.label: The day of the Lord and community care
sections.note: 1 Thessalonians 5 discusses the day of the Lord, watchfulness, and care within the community; the chapter is exhortative and apocalyptic.

sections.label: Thanks and endurance under pressure
sections.note: 2 Thessalonians 1 thanks the community for faith and endurance and speaks of divine judgment. This is pastoral correspondence, not a report of travel.

sections.label: Clarification about the day of the Lord
sections.note: 2 Thessalonians 2 addresses confusion about the day of the Lord and urges steadiness. The chapter uses apocalyptic language without locating a route or scene.

sections.label: Prayer, work, and steadfastness
sections.note: 2 Thessalonians 3 requests prayer and instructs the community about work and orderly conduct. The advice concerns shared life rather than travel; it does not document a meeting location.

sections.label: Sound teaching and prayer
sections.note: 1 Timothy 1–2 warns against disruptive teaching and gives instruction about prayer and community conduct. The letter addresses Timothy; it does not identify the setting in which these instructions were given.

sections.label: Leadership and godliness
sections.note: 1 Timothy 3–4 discusses qualifications for overseers and servants and calls for disciplined teaching. These are instructions for church life, not travel narration; it does not name a specific gathering site.

sections.label: Care, conduct, and final charge
sections.note: 1 Timothy 5–6 addresses care for widows, elders, conduct, and the dangers of wealth. The material is pastoral guidance.

sections.label: Memory and courage
sections.note: 2 Timothy 1 recalls faith, calls Timothy to courage, and refers to hardship and confinement. The chapter does not establish the precise setting of the correspondence.

sections.label: Teaching and endurance
sections.note: 2 Timothy 2 uses images of a soldier, athlete, and farmer to urge endurance and faithful teaching; these are metaphors rather than reported events.

sections.label: Scripture and the final charge
sections.note: 2 Timothy 3–4 commends scripture, gives a final charge, and closes with personal greetings. The correspondence names people but does not supply a complete location record; it does not supply a complete location record or itinerary.

sections.label: Elders and sound teaching
sections.note: Titus 1 instructs Titus about appointing elders and addressing harmful teaching. It refers to communities in Crete but gives no itinerary or precise meeting place.

sections.label: Teaching for community life
sections.note: Titus 2 gives instruction for different members of the community and grounds conduct in the grace of God. The text does not identify a specific household.

sections.label: Good works and closing instructions
sections.note: Titus 3 urges civic conduct and good works and closes with travel-related plans and greetings. Plans do not confirm completed travel.

sections.label: An appeal for welcome
sections.note: Philemon is a brief personal letter that thanks God for the recipient’s faith and appeals for Onesimus to be welcomed as a brother. The closing mentions hospitality and travel plans, not a confirmed route.

sections.label: The Son and the promised rest
sections.note: Hebrews 1–4 presents the Son, compares him with angels and Moses, and warns the hearers to enter God’s rest through scriptural argument and exhortation.

sections.label: The priesthood and Melchizedek
sections.note: Hebrews 5–7 develops the high-priest theme through Melchizedek and scriptural interpretation. The argument is literary and theological; it does not place the audience at a reconstructable sanctuary scene.

sections.label: Covenant, sanctuary, and sacrifice
sections.note: Hebrews 8–10 contrasts covenant and sanctuary language and discusses sacrifice and access to God. The sanctuary imagery draws on scripture; the text does not locate its audience at a physical sanctuary.

sections.label: Faith and perseverance
sections.note: Hebrews 11–13 recalls figures of faith and urges perseverance, mutual care, and steadfastness. The historical examples span many places and times; they are not one itinerary for the letter’s audience.

sections.label: Trials, wisdom, and hearing
sections.note: James 1 addresses trials, wisdom, hearing and doing the word, and care for the vulnerable among dispersed communities.

sections.label: Faith without partiality
sections.note: James 2 challenges favoritism and connects faith with action, using examples from scripture. Its assembly language suggests community life but does not identify a particular building or route.

sections.label: Speech, patience, and prayer
sections.note: James 3–5 treats speech, conflict, patience, prayer, and care for the sick.

sections.label: Living hope and a chosen people
sections.note: 1 Peter 1–2 addresses scattered believers with language of living hope, holiness, and a chosen people; the audience description is broad and does not give a travel route.

sections.label: Conduct, suffering, and service
sections.note: 1 Peter 3–4 gives household and community instruction and speaks of suffering and service. The counsel is not tied to one narrated event; the text does not specify a particular household setting.

sections.label: Care and steadfastness
sections.note: 1 Peter 5 instructs elders and the community to care for one another and remain steadfast. The chapter addresses elders and community care but does not state an exact gathering place or route.

sections.label: Knowledge, growth, and testimony
sections.note: 2 Peter 1 urges growth in virtue and recalls the transfiguration as testimony. The chapter refers to a past event but does not narrate its location in detail.

sections.label: Warnings and the promised day
sections.note: 2 Peter 2–3 warns against false teachers and discusses the promised day of the Lord. Its judgment imagery is theological and future-facing.

sections.label: Life, light, and fellowship
sections.note: 1 John 1–2 speaks of the message heard, fellowship, light, obedience, and love. It is a pastoral argument without travel narration.

sections.label: Love and discernment
sections.note: 1 John 3–4 connects love of one another with discernment about testimony concerning Jesus. The chapters offer communal teaching rather than a geographic episode.

sections.label: Faith and assurance
sections.note: 1 John 5 emphasizes belief, testimony, life, and assurance. It closes as pastoral instruction rather than a journey or location account.

sections.label: Truth, love, and discernment
sections.note: 2 John is a short letter urging the recipient community to walk in truth and love and to discern its teachers. The address does not securely identify a named city or building.

sections.label: Hospitality and faithful witness
sections.note: 3 John commends hospitality toward traveling coworkers and contrasts it with a leader’s refusal to receive them. The letter names people but not a secure modern location; its travel references are not a complete route.

sections.label: Contend for the faith
sections.note: Jude urges its recipients to contend for the faith, warns against corrupt teaching, and closes with praise. Its references to earlier scriptural judgments are examples, not one contemporary setting.

sections.label: Opening vision and messages to the churches
sections.note: Revelation 1–3 presents an opening vision and messages addressed to seven churches. The named communities are real places in the text, but this sequence is visionary rather than a travel route.

sections.label: The throne, scroll, and seals
sections.note: Revelation 4–7 depicts visions of the throne, the scroll and seals, and a multitude. These are visionary scenes rather than earthly travel stops.

sections.label: Trumpets and witnesses
sections.note: Revelation 8–11 unfolds trumpet visions and witness imagery. The sequence is apocalyptic symbolism, not a route across mapped terrain.

sections.label: Conflict, beasts, and bowls
sections.note: Revelation 12–16 depicts a woman, dragon, beasts, and bowls in symbolic visions, not geographic descriptions.

sections.label: Babylon and the rider
sections.note: Revelation 17–19 portrays Babylon and the rider through apocalyptic imagery and judgment scenes. Babylon functions within the vision’s symbolic world; the section is not a travel account.

sections.label: Final judgment and the new creation
sections.note: Revelation 20–22 presents final judgment, a new heaven and earth, and the vision of the holy city. These are eschatological visions, not geographic descriptions of a present-day place.
